q.intro.text: A square garden is x feet on each side. You make it three feet longer and three feet wider, so it is still a square, x plus three feet on each side.

q.ask.text: Its new area is x plus three, squared, in square feet. Which polynomial gives the same area, for every x? Pick one, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the box fills first, then the algebra.

e.s0.text: A square is a quantity times itself. So x plus three, squared, is x plus three times x plus three. Both sides of the box are x plus three.

e.s1.text: Every term times every term. x times x is x squared. x times three is three x, and three times x is three x again. Three times three is nine. Four partial products: four pieces of the garden.

e.s2.text: The two three x pieces are like terms, with the same power of x, so they collect: six x. x plus three, squared, is x squared plus six x plus nine. A quadratic trinomial.

e.s3.text: Check with x equal to two. Five squared is twenty five, and four plus twelve plus nine is twenty five. It checks. But x squared plus nine gives thirteen. It leaves out the two strips.

e.why.text: Quick check. Where does the six x come from?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. Two of the four partial products are three x, and like terms add: six x.

e.w-fn.text: Squaring a sum is not squaring each term. x plus three, squared, is x plus three times x plus three. The two strips are real area.

e.w-unlike.text: x and three are unlike terms. They never combine. The six x is two strips of three x, each three feet by x feet.

t.intro.text: Now a bigger product: x minus two, times x squared plus x plus three. Two terms times three terms: a box with six cells. The first row is done for you.

t.row.text: Your step: the second row. What is negative two times each term of x squared plus x plus three?

t.r-ok.text: Yes. Negative two multiplies every term across the top. Six partial products in all.

t.r-part.text: Negative two multiplies every term across the top, not only the first one.

t.r-sign.text: A negative times a positive is negative. Negative two times x squared is negative two x squared.

t.x2.text: Now collect. The x squared cells sit on one diagonal: x squared, and negative two x squared. What is the coefficient of x squared?

t.x2-ok.text: Yes. x squared minus two x squared is negative x squared. The coefficient is negative one.

t.x2-one.text: There are two x squared cells: x squared from the first row, and negative two x squared from the second. Add both.

t.x2-sign.text: One plus negative two is negative one, not one.

t.x2-no.text: Add the coefficients of the two x squared cells: one, and negative two.

t.x1.text: And the x cells: three x, and negative two x. What is the coefficient of x?

t.x1-ok.text: Yes. Three x minus two x is x. So the product is x cubed minus x squared plus x minus six.

t.x1-no.text: Add the coefficients of the two x cells: three, and negative two.

t.deg.text: Last one. What is the degree of x cubed minus x squared plus x minus six?

t.d-ok.text: Yes. Degree three: a cubic polynomial with four terms. Every term times every term, then collect by power.

t.d-count.text: Four is the number of terms. The degree is the highest power, x cubed.

t.d-sum.text: Do not add the exponents. The degree is the largest one.

t.d-no.text: Find the highest power of x among the terms.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked x squared plus six x plus nine, and you were right. Now you can show why: every term times every term.

t.cb-fn.text: At the start you picked x squared plus nine. That squares each term, and leaves out the cross products: the two strips.

t.cb-double.text: At the start you picked two x plus six. That doubles, instead of squaring. A square is a product of two equal factors.

t.cb-none.text: Every term times every term, then collect by power. That is how every polynomial product comes out.

p.intro.text: Riley subtracts. Five x squared plus three x minus two, minus the quantity two x squared minus four x plus one. Riley gets three x squared minus x minus one. Is Riley right?

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because, with the reason that makes the line true.

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.c1.text: Right. At x equal to one, the left side is six minus negative one, which is seven. But Riley's answer is one. One value where they differ is enough.

p.c2.text: Right. The minus multiplies every term: negative two x squared, plus four x, minus one. Riley flipped only the first sign.

p.c3.text: Right. Collect by power. Five x squared minus two x squared is three x squared. Three x plus four x is seven x. Negative two minus one is negative three.

p.no.exc.text: A rewrite has to hold for every x. One value where it fails is a counterexample, not an exception.

p.no.first.text: That is exactly Riley's slip. The minus is in front of the whole group, so it multiplies every term.

p.no.ex.text: Matching values never prove a rewrite for every x. And here, the values do not even match.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That's a proof. A counterexample shows Riley's line is wrong, and the opposite of the whole polynomial gives three x squared plus seven x minus three.
